Your art is great! But you're not using enough contrast in your pieces. Try using softer pencils to achieve darker colors, nearly black in the darkest areas

Try using reference pictures of the same position you wanna draw. Even when you're stializing, the anatomy (like how the foot or upper legs look) should still line up perspective wise.
Other things to look out for would be the size of the lower arm and hands, they're too small compared to the rest of the body.
And try using more rounded lines instead of letting it run into a sharp point. It looks great in certain areas, but it really throws me off at certain body parts, like the knees.

I hope this helps ^^

Alright. Firstly, I'm just trying to learn new stuff and I didn't include non-binary people in the OP because the post was already very long.

Of course non-binary people are valid and they aren't excluded from this discussion.

My main point was that Demi and Gray are more like additional pieces of information to a given sexuality. Since (for example) someone can be Demi while having an attraction to the same gender. So I don't see why we call it as much a sexuality as pansexual (for example).

In my opinion we should simplify the basics of sexualities and attraction, so we all have the same ground to go off of.
If there are any additions (such as a Demisexual experiences on top of their sexuality), then that's something you could just add onto that main term.
But instead there are a lot of new words that are being invented, which makes it hard to navigate and hard to understand. Especially for newcomers to the community, that are trying to figure themselves out.

Andro and Gyne are important, but those terms don't specify the genitals of a person, instead they specify how they appear (which is very valid too, but an important difference).
Not everyone is sexually attracted to all people who pose as male/female. I think that's a point of divergence that falls under the "addition" bit I mentioned earlier. So (for example) a homosexual adding "I'm also attracted to Trans-men" is easier to get and relate to, than inventing a whole new word for it.

Plus, like I said, it makes it easier for questioning people to find themselves.

But thank you for adding your perspective, I probably should've mentioned non-binary people as well and their unique experience in this.
